case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal district court may excuse (via equitable tolling or other equitable exceptions) the 30-day deadline to remove a case from state to federal court under 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b)(1).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b)(1) (the 30-day time limit for filing a notice of removal after receipt of the initial pleading), within the broader federal removal scheme (28 U.S.C. §§ 1441–1455).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Enbridge argues that § 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day removal deadline is a nonjurisdictional, procedural time bar that—like most limitations periods—carries a rebuttable presumption of equitable tolling/exception. They contend Congress did not clearly preclude equitable tolling in the text, and that the Court’s general approach to nonjurisdictional deadlines allows equitable relief in extraordinary circumstances. Enbridge and supporting amici further stress that this dispute implicates uniquely federal interests (interstate/international energy infrastructure, treaty-related issues, and federal preemption), making it especially appropriate for federal adjudication even if removal was late.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Michigan argues that § 1446(b)(1) is not a run-of-the-mill statute of limitations but a tightly integrated, congressionally calibrated forum-allocation rule that historically has been strictly construed and strictly enforced. Michigan maintains that the removal statute’s structure includes multiple specific, enumerated timing rules and exceptions—some expressly allowing extensions for cause—showing Congress considered timing flexibility and chose limited exceptions, leaving no room for courts to invent additional equitable exceptions. Michigan also emphasizes practical/administrability concerns: allowing equitable tolling would inject fact-bound satellite litigation into what Congress designed as a quick, predictable threshold process. Finally, Michigan points out that, on the Sixth Circuit’s findings, Enbridge was extraordinarily late (roughly 850 days) and missed multiple opportunities, and that Enbridge did not seek Supreme Court review of the Sixth Circuit’s case-specific determination that no equitable basis existed even if such authority were available.
key_precedents: Arellano v. McDonough (equitable-tolling presumptions and when Congress rebuts them)
Nutraceutical Corp. v. Lambert (limits on equitable tolling/extension of certain procedural deadlines)
Young v. United States (equitable tolling principles in the bankruptcy/tax context)

John Roberts.reasoning: The strongest petitioner argument remains the Irwin/Arellano presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are equitably tollable, but—as Justice Kagan persuasively emphasizes—the structure of § 1446 supplies multiple timing triggers and targeted exceptions (including later-ascertainability and the express bad-faith carveout), which is powerful evidence Congress already calibrated the only flexibility it wanted. Nutraceutical, cited by several colleagues, reinforces that when a deadline is embedded in a tightly reticulated procedural scheme designed for speed and administrability, courts should not treat it as malleable through equity absent textual warrant. I also find Justice Gorsuch’s federalism point significant: removal alters the ordinary state–federal allocation, and adding judge-made tolling would expand removal beyond the conditions Congress specified while inviting fact-bound satellite litigation inconsistent with § 1447(c)’s prompt remand mechanism. A narrow holding—no equitable tolling of § 1446(b)(1) when the plaintiff timely objects—best respects precedent, statutory design, and institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest contention remains Irwin/Arellano’s presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are equitably tollable, but that background rule yields when Congress’s text and design indicate otherwise. As Justice Kagan explains, § 1446’s integrated timing architecture—including § 1446(b)(3)’s later-ascertainability trigger and § 1446(c)(1)’s express bad-faith exception—shows Congress specified the only flexibility it wanted, leaving no warrant for a freestanding equitable overlay. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Nutraceutical is persuasive under a textualist approach: when a deadline is embedded in a tightly reticulated procedural scheme designed for speed and administrability, courts should not treat it as “malleable” absent textual authorization. Because removal alters the federal–state forum allocation and § 1446(b)(1) commands that the notice “shall be filed within 30 days,” I see no legitimate basis to extend that period through judge-made tolling when the plaintiff timely invokes the defect under § 1447(c).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioners’ strongest point remains the Irwin/Arellano presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are ordinarily equitably tollable, but I agree with Justice Kagan that § 1446’s tightly reticulated timing scheme—complete with later-ascertainability in § 1446(b)(3) and the express bad-faith exception in § 1446(c)(1)—rebuts any background presumption by showing Congress already specified the flexibility it wanted. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Nutraceutical is persuasive on administrability and structure: importing tolling here would convert a rule-like removal gate into fact-bound threshold litigation over diligence and extraordinary circumstances, undermining Congress’s predictable forum-allocation design and § 1447(c)’s prompt-remand mechanism. Even if the deadline is claim-processing rather than jurisdictional, that only means it can be forfeited; it does not authorize courts to extend it through an atextual equitable overlay when the plaintiff timely objects. Nothing in colleagues’ discussion identifies statutory text or precedent that genuinely compels tolling in this removal context, so I remain with the Respondent.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest petitioner argument remains the Irwin/Arellano presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are equitably tollable, particularly where fairness concerns are acute, but in this removal context that presumption is rebutted by Congress’s unusually detailed timing architecture. Justice Kagan’s point about § 1446’s built-in safety valves—especially later-ascertainability in § 1446(b)(3) and the express bad-faith exception in § 1446(c)(1)—persuades me that Congress specified where equity-like flexibility belongs, leaving no gap for a free-floating tolling doctrine. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Nutraceutical reinforces the administrability concern: importing tolling would trigger threshold “satellite litigation” over diligence and extraordinary circumstances in a federalism-sensitive forum-allocation scheme, undermining speed and predictability. While my pragmatic instincts are sympathetic to tolling in cases of genuine obstruction, the statutory design here channels those concerns into targeted provisions, so I do not see a principled basis to add judge-made tolling when the plaintiff timely invokes § 1447(c).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest petitioner argument remains the Irwin/Arellano presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are equitably tollable, but the text-and-structure of § 1446 rebut it: this is not a free-standing limitations period but a tightly reticulated, front-end forum-allocation mechanism with specified triggers and calibrated exceptions. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Nutraceutical strengthens the workability point that importing equitable tolling would turn a rule-like 30-day gate into fact-bound satellite litigation over diligence and “extraordinary circumstances,” contrary to Congress’s evident preference for speed and predictability. Justice Barrett’s emphasis on the statute’s built-in safety valves—especially later-ascertainability and the bad-faith exception—persuasively shows Congress addressed equitable concerns in targeted ways, suggesting no residual invitation for a judge-made tolling overlay. Even if the deadline is nonjurisdictional, § 1447(c)’s remand-on-timely-objection mechanism confirms the design choice that courts enforce this procedural defect when properly raised rather than rebalancing it through equity.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains the Irwin/Arellano presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are equitably tollable, but as Justice Kagan persuasively notes, § 1446 is not a freestanding limitations period—it is a tightly integrated forum-allocation scheme with specified triggers and express safety valves, including § 1446(b)(3) and § 1446(c)(1)’s bad-faith exception. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Nutraceutical reinforces my view that, even when a deadline is nonjurisdictional, the surrounding structure can make it effectively unalterable where Congress has built a rule-like, administrable timing architecture and provided the exclusive exceptions it wanted. The opposing argument does not supply a textual hook for an additional, judge-made tolling regime, and in removal—where federalism and predictability are central—adding an open-ended equitable overlay would expand federal jurisdictional access beyond the conditions Congress set. I therefore remain convinced the statute’s design rebuts any default tolling presumption here when the plaintiff timely objects under § 1447(c).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains the Irwin/Arellano presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are equitably tollable, but in this context the statutory text and structure supply the clear rebuttal: § 1446’s 30-day command is embedded in a tightly reticulated, front-end forum-allocation scheme with specific alternative triggers and express exceptions. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on administrability and legitimacy concerns is persuasive—equitable tolling would convert a rule-like removal gateway into fact-bound satellite litigation over diligence and “extraordinary circumstances,” undermining Congress’s design for speed and predictability, reinforced by § 1447(c)’s remand-on-timely-objection mechanism. Justice Kagan’s and Justice Barrett’s reliance on Nutraceutical strengthens the point that even nonjurisdictional deadlines can be effectively “unalterable” when Congress has crafted a detailed procedural framework with calibrated safety valves (including later-ascertainability and the bad-faith carveout). No colleague has identified precedent requiring tolling here notwithstanding such structural evidence, so I see no principled basis to create a judge-made equitable exception to § 1446(b)(1) in the face of a timely remand motion.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains the Irwin/Arellano presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are equitably tollable, but I do not think it survives the specific statutory design here. As Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, § 1446 supplies multiple timing triggers and calibrated exceptions (including § 1446(b)(3) and § 1446(c)(1)’s bad-faith provision), which is powerful structural evidence that Congress specified the flexibility it wanted and left no gap for a freestanding equitable-tolling overlay. Nutraceutical, which several colleagues invoke, reinforces that even nonjurisdictional deadlines can be effectively “unalterable” when embedded in a rule-like, administrable procedural scheme—especially one allocating authority between state and federal courts and enforced via § 1447(c)’s remand mechanism. Because tolling would invite fact-bound satellite litigation at the forum-allocation threshold and expand removal beyond the conditions Congress wrote, I would enforce the 30-day rule when a plaintiff timely objects.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioners’ best point remains the Irwin/Arellano presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are ordinarily equitably tollable to avoid unfairness, but in this setting I agree with Justice Kagan that § 1446’s tightly calibrated timing architecture—including later-ascertainability in (b)(3) and the express bad-faith exception in (c)(1)—rebuts any default equitable overlay. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Nutraceutical is persuasive for pragmatic reasons: importing tolling would convert a front-end, rule-like forum-allocation gate into fact-bound satellite litigation about diligence and “extraordinary circumstances,” undermining procedural fairness and predictability for both sides. Even accepting the deadline is nonjurisdictional, § 1447(c)’s remand-on-timely-objection mechanism indicates Congress wanted courts to enforce this procedural defect when properly raised, not to redesign the scheme through equity. On these extreme facts of very late removal, the practical consequences and federalism-sensitive structure counsel sticking to the statute’s administrable rule rather than recognizing an atextual tolling doctrine.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day removal deadline is a nonjurisdictional claims-processing rule, but the removal scheme is a congressionally calibrated forum-allocation framework that Congress designed to be fast and predictable, reinforced by § 1447(c)’s direction to remand upon timely objection to removal defects. Under Nutraceutical Corp. v. Lambert, even nonjurisdictional deadlines are not subject to equitable tolling when the text and structure make the timing mandatory and the surrounding scheme supplies specific, limited exceptions—here, § 1446 contains multiple express timing provisions and targeted exceptions (e.g., § 1446(b)(3), (c)), indicating Congress chose when flexibility is allowed. Arellano v. McDonough’s presumption of equitable tolling is rebutted in this context because the statutory structure and history show Congress did not invite judicially created equitable exceptions in removal timing, where strict construction has long protected federalism and state-court competence. A narrow holding rejecting equitable tolling for § 1446(b)(1) best preserves administrability and institutional legitimacy by enforcing the lines Congress drew rather than inviting fact-bound satellite litigation over removal timeliness.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) provides that the notice of removal “shall be filed within 30 days,” and in the removal context Congress has created a tightly reticulated, forum-allocation scheme in §§1441–1455 that courts must apply as written, not supplement with free-floating equitable exceptions. The statute’s broader structure contains multiple specific timing rules and enumerated exceptions (including provisions that define when the 30 days begins and other express allowances for extension in particular settings), which is strong textual evidence that Congress calibrated the limited circumstances for flexibility and left no gap for judge-made tolling. Consistent with Nutraceutical Corp. v. Lambert, where the Court refused equitable tolling for a procedural deadline embedded in a detailed scheme, courts should not graft equitable tolling onto §1446(b)(1)’s removal deadline. Even if the deadline is nonjurisdictional, that does not license courts to rewrite Congress’s conditions for invoking a federal forum, particularly where federal jurisdiction and state-court primacy absent proper removal are at stake.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) provides that a defendant “shall” file a notice of removal within 30 days, and in the removal context that command operates as a mandatory, party-invoked claim-processing rule that courts may not alter when properly raised. Under Nutraceutical Corp. v. Lambert, even a nonjurisdictional deadline is not subject to equitable tolling where the text and overall scheme show an intent to preclude judicially created flexibility; here, the removal statutes supply a detailed, integrated set of timing rules and enumerated exceptions, indicating Congress chose specific and limited departure points rather than an open-ended equitable safety valve. Allowing equitable tolling would undermine Congress’s forum-allocation design by inviting fact-bound satellite litigation and uncertainty into what is meant to be a quick, predictable threshold determination. Whatever federal interests petitioners invoke, courts must apply the removal scheme Congress enacted, not expand removal through equitable exceptions absent a clearer textual basis.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) uses mandatory language—notice of removal “shall” be filed within 30 days—within a carefully calibrated forum-allocation scheme where Congress also provided specific timing rules and enumerated exceptions elsewhere in the removal statute, signaling limited judicial power to add extra equitable carveouts. Under Nutraceutical Corp. v. Lambert, even nonjurisdictional deadlines can be “mandatory claim-processing rules” that are not subject to equitable tolling when the statute’s text and structure show Congress intended strict enforcement. Whatever the Irwin/Arellano equitable-tolling presumption might be in benefits or limitations contexts, it fits poorly here because the consequence is not loss of a merits forum—state court remains open—while expanding equitable exceptions would invite fact-bound satellite litigation that undermines Congress’s interest in prompt, predictable removal decisions. I would therefore hold district courts lack authority to excuse § 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day deadline via equitable tolling or similar equitable exceptions when timely objection is made.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day window is part of an integrated removal scheme that allocates forum choice and is designed to be quick and predictable, with § 1447(c) requiring remand when procedural removal defects are timely raised. Even assuming the deadline is nonjurisdictional, the statute’s structure—including multiple built-in timing rules and specific safety valves (e.g., § 1446(b)(3)’s later-ascertainability provision and § 1446(c)(1)’s express bad-faith exception for late diversity removals)—rebuts any background presumption of equitable tolling under Arellano v. McDonough. As in Nutraceutical Corp. v. Lambert, where the Court refused to treat a carefully calibrated procedural deadline as “malleable in every respect,” reading judge-made equitable exceptions into § 1446(b)(1) would undermine workability by inviting fact-bound satellite litigation at the threshold of removal. Congress showed it knew how to authorize extensions and equitable flexibility in this area, and it did so in limited, specified ways—so courts should not add a general equitable-tolling overlay to § 1446(b)(1).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) sets a firm, congressionally prescribed 30-day period to invoke a federal forum, and the removal statutes are to be strictly construed because they alter the ordinary allocation of judicial power between state and federal courts. Even assuming § 1446(b)(1) is nonjurisdictional, the statute’s text and structure rebut any background presumption of equitable tolling: Congress built multiple specific timing rules and express safety valves (including § 1446(b)(3)’s later-ascertainability provision and § 1446(c)(1)’s “bad faith” exception), leaving no gap for judge-made extensions. That approach accords with Nutraceutical Corp. v. Lambert, which refused equitable tolling where the procedural scheme was comprehensive and did not authorize judicial enlargement, and with Arellano v. McDonough, which treats numerous express exceptions as strong evidence Congress meant to preclude additional equitable ones. Allowing equitable tolling here would invite case-by-case balancing in a threshold, time-sensitive forum-allocation scheme Congress designed to be predictable and quickly administered.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day removal deadline operates as a congressionally calibrated, rule-like forum-allocation provision within an integrated removal scheme, and we should be reluctant to graft an extra-textual equitable exception onto that framework. As in Nutraceutical Corp. v. Lambert, the text and structure signal a mandatory deadline not subject to judge-made tolling where Congress has specified detailed timing rules and enumerated exceptions elsewhere in the statutory scheme, favoring predictable and administrable threshold determinations. That conclusion accords with the removal statute’s longstanding history of strict construction and strict enforcement, and it avoids the practical problems of fact-bound “satellite litigation” over diligence and extraordinary circumstances at the removal stage. Even if one started from the equitable-tolling framework discussed in Arellano v. McDonough, the removal statute’s design rebuts any presumption by demonstrating Congress’s choice of limited, express exceptions rather than open-ended equitable discretion.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) directs that a notice of removal “shall be filed within 30 days,” and in the removal context that deadline functions as a congressionally calibrated forum-allocation rule within a detailed statutory scheme (28 U.S.C. §§ 1441–1455), not a free-floating limitations period. Even if the 30-day limit is nonjurisdictional, it is a mandatory claim-processing rule that must be enforced when properly invoked, and the structure of the removal statutes—containing multiple specific timing provisions and limited, enumerated exceptions—rebuts any background presumption of judge-made equitable tolling. Nutraceutical Corp. v. Lambert supports treating similarly mandatory, scheme-embedded deadlines as not subject to equitable tolling where the text and structure indicate inflexibility, and that reasoning fits § 1446(b)(1) especially given Congress’s evident interest in speed and administrability in removal.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Although § 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day deadline is nonjurisdictional, it functions as a mandatory claim-processing rule within a tightly structured, front-end forum-allocation scheme, and Congress’s detailed timing architecture (including multiple enumerated exceptions and provisions that expressly permit extensions for cause) is sufficient to rebut any default equitable-tolling presumption. As Nutraceutical Corp. v. Lambert explains, nonjurisdictional deadlines can still be “unalterable” when the statutory text and structure indicate Congress meant strict enforcement, and § 1446(b)(1)’s command that a notice of removal “shall” be filed within 30 days reflects that design choice. Allowing equitable tolling here would undermine procedural fairness to plaintiffs and administrability by inviting fact-bound satellite litigation over threshold removal timing, contrary to Congress’s evident intent for a short, predictable removal process. On these facts, where the removal attempt was extraordinarily late, preserving predictable enforcement best serves practical consequences and the integrity of the procedural scheme Congress enacted.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal district court may apply equitable exceptions (e.g., equitable tolling) to excuse a defendant’s failure to file a notice of removal within 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day deadline.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b)(1) (30-day procedural time limit for removal of a civil action) and related removal scheme provisions (including statutory exceptions elsewhere in § 1446).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Enbridge argues that § 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day removal deadline should be treated like a limitations-type filing rule that presumptively incorporates equitable tolling/other equitable exceptions unless Congress clearly says otherwise. Petitioners contend the Sixth Circuit wrongly treated the deadline as categorically inflexible, and they point to the Court’s general approach to filing deadlines—often allowing equitable doctrines absent a clear statement to foreclose them. They also emphasize that removal is an important statutory right and that rigidly enforcing the 30-day limit can unfairly defeat that right in unusual circumstances, so district courts should retain authority to excuse noncompliance when equity warrants it.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Michigan argues that § 1446(b)(1) is a procedural, forum-allocation rule within a comprehensive removal framework—historically strictly enforced—and not a statute of limitations designed to be softened by equitable tolling. Respondent stresses that Congress expressly created multiple specific exceptions and extensions within the removal statute, indicating courts should not invent additional, atextual exceptions. Michigan also argues that allowing equitable exceptions would undermine the removal scheme’s goals of speed, predictability, and minimal fact-bound satellite litigation over forum choice, and that missing the removal deadline is not analogous to losing a merits claim because defendants still have a forum (state court) to litigate.

John Roberts.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains the default presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines can be equitably tolled to prevent unfair forfeiture or manipulation, but § 1446’s text and structure rebut that presumption by supplying a detailed set of timing triggers and expressly enumerated adjustments. Justice Barrett’s observation that multiple specific statutory exceptions “heighten the structural inference” against additional judge-made tolling (consistent with Arellano) reinforces that, under Nutraceutical, the relevant question is whether Congress left “room” for equitable flexibility—and this scheme reads as calibrated and exclusive. Justice Alito’s administrability concern also matters to institutional legitimacy: tolling would predictably spawn fact-bound satellite litigation over forum choice, frustrating Congress’s evident aim of speed and predictability in removal while leaving defendants a full merits forum in state court. I would keep the holding narrow: equitable tolling is unavailable for § 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day deadline at least where the plaintiff timely raises the defect under § 1447(c), without opining on other doctrines not presented.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains the general presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines can be equitably tolled, particularly to prevent gamesmanship, but that presumption gives way when Congress has spoken through a detailed statutory design. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Nutraceutical properly frames the inquiry: whether § 1446’s text and structure “leave room” for judge-made flexibility, and the reticulated timing scheme—paired with the specific adjustments and exceptions Justice Barrett highlights (consistent with Arellano’s ‘heightened structural inference’)—indicates exclusivity. In the removal context, as Justice Kavanaugh notes, equitable tolling would expand the availability of a federal forum beyond the precise limits Congress set in a federalism-sensitive allocation of authority, contrary to strict construction of removal statutes. No colleague’s points undermine the textual inference that courts may not add an atextual tolling exception to § 1446(b)(1) when the plaintiff timely invokes the defect under § 1447(c).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains the general presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are subject to equitable tolling, but § 1446’s text and reticulated structure rebut that presumption by specifying multiple timing triggers and discrete exceptions—leaving no “room” for additional judge-made tolling. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Arellano strengthens the negative-inference analysis: when Congress enumerates particular exceptions (as in § 1446(b)(3) and (c)), it heightens the structural inference against implied ones. Chief Justice Roberts is also right on practical consequences: tolling would invite fact-bound satellite litigation over forum choice and undermine Congress’s evident preference for speed and administrability in removal, especially where the defendant still receives a merits forum in state court. Nothing I’ve heard supplies a textual hook or a limiting principle that would confine equitable tolling to truly extraordinary cases without effectively rewriting the calibrated statutory scheme.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point—the usual equitable-tolling presumption for nonjurisdictional deadlines to prevent unfair forfeiture—has force when rights are lost, but here the defendant is not deprived of a merits forum; the case proceeds in state court. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Arellano, combined with Justice Kagan’s emphasis on § 1446’s tightly reticulated timing architecture and enumerated exceptions, persuades me that Congress did not “leave room” for additional judge-made tolling under Nutraceutical’s framework. While I remain sensitive to strategic manipulation that can burden vulnerable litigants, importing equitable tolling into removal would invite fact-bound satellite litigation over forum choice (as Justice Alito notes) and undermine the statute’s administrable, calibrated allocation between state and federal courts. On my pragmatic methodology, the marginal equity gain is outweighed by systemic costs and the strong structural inference that any further exceptions must come from Congress.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest petitioner argument remains the baseline presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines can be equitably tolled to prevent unfair forfeiture, especially where the plaintiff’s conduct may have obscured removability. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes through Nutraceutical, the real question is whether the text and structure “leave room” for equitable flexibility, and § 1446’s reticulated set of timing triggers and express adjustments points the other way. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Arellano strengthens that structural inference: when Congress enumerates specific exceptions within the same timing framework, it signals exclusivity and counsels against judge-made add-ons. Pragmatically, as Justice Alito notes, tolling would invite satellite litigation about forum choice rather than merits, and because a missed deadline merely keeps the case in state court, the equitable necessity is comparatively weak—so I would enforce the 30-day rule when properly invoked under § 1447(c).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains the general presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are equitably tollable, especially to deter strategic manipulation, but § 1446’s text and architecture rebut it. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Arellano is especially telling: Congress’s enumerated timing adjustments and exceptions in a tightly reticulated removal scheme “heighten the structural inference” that courts may not add atextual tolling on top. As the Chief Justice notes via Nutraceutical, the question is whether the statute leaves room for equity; here the calibrated, administrable forum-allocation rules—combined with the federalism-sensitive transfer of cases from state to federal court—counsel strict enforcement when a plaintiff timely invokes the defect under § 1447(c). Equitable tolling would invite fact-bound satellite litigation over forum choice, a cost Congress appears to have avoided by specifying the limited exceptions it wanted.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains the default presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines can be equitably tolled to prevent manipulation, but Nutraceutical and Arellano make clear the real inquiry is whether Congress’s text and structure "leave room" for that flexibility. Chief Justice Roberts’s structural point is decisive for me: § 1446 is a detailed, calibrated timing scheme with multiple express adjustments and exceptions, which strongly suggests Congress chose administrable lines over open-ended equitable add-ons. Justice Thomas’s federalism/strict-construction concern reinforces that we should be especially reluctant to expand removal beyond the precise conditions Congress specified, given removal’s sovereign-allocation consequences. And Justice Alito’s practical warning about fact-bound satellite litigation over forum choice underscores why an atextual tolling regime would undermine predictability without protecting any substantive right (defendants still have a full merits forum in state court).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Petitioner’s best argument remains the default presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines can be equitably tolled, particularly to prevent strategic manipulation, but I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that Nutraceutical reframes the inquiry: we ask whether § 1446’s text and structure leave room for flexibility. Here, the mandatory command (“shall be filed within 30 days”) operates within a tightly reticulated scheme that already supplies specific timing triggers and exceptions in § 1446(b)(3) and § 1446(c), and—consistent with Arellano as Justice Thomas and others emphasize—those enumerated exceptions create a strong negative inference against additional judge-made tolling. Justice Alito’s practical point underscores the textual conclusion: tolling would invite fact-bound satellite litigation over forum selection in a statute designed for speed and administrability, and the defendant still has a merits forum in state court. Nothing in the opposing position shows Congress intended an atextual equitable overlay for this calibrated forum-allocation mechanism, so my vote remains for Respondent.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point—the usual presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are equitably tollable to prevent unfair forfeitures—loses force in the removal setting because the consequence is not extinguishment of a claim but continuation in state court, so the equity need is comparatively weak. Justice Kagan’s Nutraceutical-based structural point most persuades me that § 1446’s tightly reticulated timing scheme (with Congress’s own targeted adjustments) leaves no “room” for an additional, judge-made tolling overlay, and Justice Barrett’s Arellano inference from enumerated exceptions reinforces that conclusion. As a pragmatic matter consistent with my methodology, Justice Alito and the Chief Justice are also right that tolling here would predictably generate fact-bound satellite litigation over forum choice, undermining Congress’s interest in speed and administrability. Absent a clearer textual hook or evidence of Congress anticipating equitable tolling in this context, the fair and workable course is to enforce the 30-day rule when the plaintiff timely invokes the defect under § 1447(c).

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day deadline operates as a claim-processing rule within a detailed, congressionally calibrated removal scheme, and the statute itself contains specific, enumerated extensions and exceptions elsewhere in § 1446 (e.g., § 1446(b)(3), (c)(1) & (3)(B)), reinforcing that courts should not add atextual equitable carve-outs. Under Nutraceutical Corp. v. Lambert, even nonjurisdictional timing rules are not subject to equitable tolling where the text, structure, and history show a “clear intent to preclude” such flexibility; the removal framework’s emphasis on speed, predictability, and minimal satellite litigation supplies that intent. Allowing equitable tolling here would invite fact-bound disputes over forum selection and risk undermining institutional legitimacy by departing from the strict, precedent-backed approach to removal procedures. Given § 1447(c)’s directive to remand for timely raised procedural defects, the proper course is to enforce Congress’s deadline as written.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) sets a clear, mandatory 30-day deadline for removal, and nothing in its text authorizes courts to add atextual equitable exceptions such as equitable tolling. Read in context, the removal statute is a comprehensive, congressionally calibrated scheme that includes specific, enumerated exceptions and extensions elsewhere in § 1446 and related provisions, which strongly indicates Congress did not leave room for courts to create additional exceptions. Our removal jurisprudence has long required strict construction of removal statutes out of respect for state sovereignty and the limited jurisdiction of the federal courts, see Shamrock Oil & Gas Corp. v. Sheets, 313 U.S. 100, 108-09 (1941), and equitable tolling here would expand federal removal jurisdiction beyond “the precise limits which the statute has defined.” Because removal reallocates adjudicatory authority between sovereigns rather than extinguishing a merits claim, the equitable-tolling presumption applicable to limitations periods does not overcome the statutory text and structure in this context.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) sets a firm 30-day deadline for removal within a detailed, congressionally crafted forum-allocation scheme, and nothing in its text authorizes courts to add equitable exceptions beyond those Congress expressly provided elsewhere in § 1446 (e.g., § 1446(c)(1), (c)(3)(B)). Under Nutraceutical Corp. v. Lambert, the question is whether the text and structure “leave room” for equitable tolling, and the removal statute’s multiple specific, enumerated extensions and exceptions are strong structural evidence that courts should not create additional atextual ones. Practical consequences reinforce that conclusion: permitting equitable tolling would invite fact-bound satellite litigation over forum choice and undermine the statute’s aim of speed and predictability, while a late-filing defendant is not deprived of a merits forum because it can litigate in state court. Consistent with the traditional strict construction of removal provisions and Congress’s choice to make remand mandatory upon timely objection, see § 1447(c), the deadline should be enforced as written.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) states a notice of removal “shall” be filed within 30 days, and within the removal statute’s tightly reticulated, forum-allocation scheme that deadline functions as a mandatory claim-processing rule that is not subject to judicially created equitable exceptions when properly invoked. Under Nutraceutical Corp. v. Lambert, the question is whether the text and structure “leave room for such flexibility”; here, Congress already built specific extensions and exceptions elsewhere in § 1446, signaling that additional atextual tolling is precluded. Unlike limitations periods that can bar a litigant’s merits claim, missing the removal deadline leaves defendants with a full forum (state court) to litigate, reducing any equitable necessity and reinforcing Congress’s interest in speed and predictability in forum selection. Given the removal scheme’s history of strict enforcement and Congress’s express tailoring of exceptions, I would not authorize open-ended equitable tolling of § 1446(b)(1).
